sm: The Williamson County Planning Commission opened its November 12 meeting with roll call and staff announcements. Item 34 was withdrawn and item 36 was on the consent agenda for deferral. Staff said the County Commission deferred the Errington Village standards and rezoning to March with direction to look at density and add public involvement, with a public meeting planned for December and a return to the commission in February. Staff reminded members of training on November 19 and welcomed new member Patty Hinton, who will abstain from votes tonight. Minutes and the consent agenda passed, with a correction that item 32 refers to Del Rio Pike. The commission then heard an update on drainage and erosion at Terra Vista, where the ponds are working well and a mail kiosk is still pending.

Staff agreed the Terra Vista drainage and erosion bond should be released until the annual review in April, and the commission raised no objection. Item 35, final plat for Ember Ridge East, also called the Villages at Triune East, covers 30 lots on 7.73 acres, with nine single family lots, 21 town home lots, private roads and about six acres of open space. Greenway trails will come in a later section. It passed on a motion and second. Item 37, a revised final plat for lot 208 of Errington Woods on 8.66 acres, drops a driveway and water tank requirement and seeks a variance because the nearest fire hydrant is 600 feet away. Staff said the fire marshal supports the variance, and it passed. Item 38 began for the Tributary subdivision.

Item 38, the final plat for Tributary section one with 39 lots on 89.63 acres off Cox Road, includes about 63 acres of open space, public roads, a greenway trail easement and a new non-traditional wastewater treatment system. It passed. The commission then reviewed the 2027 meeting schedule, with October moved for fall break and November moved a day earlier for Veterans Day. Staff asked whether members wanted to stop holding a December meeting, as other county boards do. Several members argued for keeping it, noting that December is sometimes the last step before projects start in spring and that a special meeting could be called if needed. A question about consistent submittal deadlines was raised.

Staff confirmed the deadlines were adjusted to give them enough time, and the commission approved the 2027 schedule as presented, keeping the December meeting for now. Item 40 was a discussion of a zoning framework for data centers. Staff stressed that nobody has proposed a data center in the unincorporated county, but that Mayor Marshall wants a thoughtful framework in place first, drawing on research and the state's model language. Staff explained what data centers are, noting that the land use impacts come mostly from electrical infrastructure, cooling, backup generators and fuel storage. They also described small company facilities, co-location facilities and very large hyperscale campuses, and why size categories matter.

Staff said the current zoning ordinance has no data center use, so they could be treated like warehouses or industrial uses without fitting standards. Proposed standards would cover infrastructure demands, compatibility such as noise and setbacks, site design, public safety, and ongoing monitoring and decommissioning. Staff weighed a use permitted by right, a special use through the Board of Zoning Appeals, and an overlay district, and recommended a site-specific special plan, similar to a planned unit development. The plan and its conditions would become the zoning for the property, with both the planning commission and county commission involved. This would allow enforceable commitments such as buffering, generator placement and infrastructure improvements. The framework has three parts, starting with the special plan.

The other two parts are a new heavy industrial zoning district and size tiers. Approval would be in two stages: a preliminary plan recommended by the planning commission and approved by the county commission, setting the use, scale and conditions, then a final plan with engineering details approved by the planning commission alone. The tiers are small, under 15,000 square feet, medium, from 15,000 to 75,000, and large, from 75,000 up to 200,000 square feet, with no hyperscale campuses. Small facilities could go in the Hamlet district, but not in the Errington area. Medium ones would need the 840 Center or heavy industrial district, and large ones only heavy industrial, each requiring a rezoning. Standards would grow stricter with size, and details will come next month.

Members asked about minimum separation distances, and staff said setbacks from homes and property lines will rise with size. Staff explained that the 840 Center district exists in the code but is not applied anywhere, and heavy industrial is not yet defined. A member asked why data centers could not simply be banned, and the county attorney said uses generally cannot be prohibited outright, so the county sets standards and a case by case review that can still deny a bad location. Members raised concerns about water use during water bans, electricity demand and noise from an existing facility. Staff said infrastructure studies would address water and power, and a member noted newer designs use closed loop cooling and that state rules make data centers pay for power upgrades.

A member asked whether electricity demand could raise residents' power bills. Another asked whether rezonings could go to elected officials first, and staff said the zoning ordinance requires the planning commission to hear and recommend first, since the special plan becomes the zoning. Members praised the process and the county commission's role as a checkpoint. Suggestions included considering fencing and lighting for security, clarifying what counts toward square footage when outbuildings exist, coordinating with other municipalities in the county, and remembering that terrorism concerns have led to retrofits elsewhere. One member said it is hard to set fixed numbers because the technology changes quickly, and supported the planned unit development approach. Another asked whether heavy industrial zoning fits the long term land use plan.

A member asked what else the new approach might open the door for. Another asked how the county would coordinate with state or federal rules, recalling how the state limited local control over cell towers. Staff said the criteria will follow the state's model regulations, that bills may be filed and federal preemption has been discussed, but for now the county remains the regulating authority. Staff said the special plan would initially apply to data centers only. On growth boundaries, staff said Hamlet zoning is not within urban growth boundaries and rezonings there would need city agreement first. The Hamlet district was chosen for small facilities because it historically allows light commercial and industrial uses up to 15,000 square feet. Staff will add detail on heavy industrial zoning next month, and the meeting adjourned.
